title: Given a set of intervals each with a start and an end, determine whether any two of them overlap. Solve it with the sort-then-adjacent-check merge-intervals pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.
shortTitle: Overlapping Intervals (Determine If Any Two Intervals Overlap)

s1_definition.profdef: This problem asks whether any pair of intervals in a set overlaps, returning a simple yes or no. It is solved by sorting the intervals by start value and then checking only adjacent pairs in the sorted order: if any interval's start is strictly before the previous interval's end, an overlap exists. Sorting reduces the all-pairs question to a single linear adjacency scan, giving n log n total time.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh has a set of booking windows for a shared settlement resource and must confirm that none of them clash, because two concurrent bookings of the same exclusive resource would be a conflict. He lines the windows up by start time, then only needs to check each window against the one right before it, since after sorting any clash must involve neighbours.
s1_definition.oneliner: Sort by start, then if any interval starts before the previous one ends, there is an overlap.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This problem asks whether any pair of intervals in a set overlaps, returning a simple yes or no. It is solved by sorting the intervals by start value and then checking only adjacent pairs in the sorted order: if any interval's start is strictly before the previous interval's end, an overlap exists. Sorting reduces the all-pairs question to a single linear adjacency scan, giving n log n total time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, Rajesh has a set of booking windows for a shared settlement resource and must confirm that none of them clash, because two concurrent bookings of the same exclusive resource would be a conflict. He lines the windows up by start time, then only needs to check each window against the one right before it, since after sorting any clash must involve neighbours.

**One line to remember:** Sort by start, then if any interval starts before the previous one ends, there is an overlap.

sections.s2_technical:
The naive approach compares every pair of intervals, which is quadratic. The key realization is that after sorting the intervals by their start value, any overlap must occur between two intervals that are adjacent in the sorted order, or at least will be detected by comparing adjacent intervals. This is because if interval A comes before interval B in start order and they overlap, then B starts before A ends, and this relationship surfaces when we compare each interval to its immediate predecessor.

So we sort by start and then walk the sorted list from the second interval onward, comparing each interval to the previous one. The overlap test is whether the current interval's start is strictly less than the previous interval's end, written `if (current.start < previous.end) return true;`. We use strictly less than when touching intervals, where the current start equals the previous end, are considered non-overlapping, which is common for booking windows where one ending exactly as the next begins is allowed. If the domain treats touching as a clash, we use less than or equal to instead.

An important subtlety is which end we compare against. After sorting by start, the previous interval in iteration order has the smaller or equal start, but its end could be larger than the current interval's end if the current is contained within the previous. Comparing the current start to the previous end correctly catches this containment case too, because a contained interval starts before the enclosing interval ends. The senior-level nuance is that we compare against the previous interval's end specifically, and if we wanted to handle a run of intervals we would track the running maximum end, but for a pure any-overlap existence check comparing to the immediate predecessor's end after sorting is sufficient because we return on the first clash.

We return false only after the full scan finds no adjacent overlap. The time complexity is n log n dominated by the sort, with the adjacency scan linear, and the space complexity is O(1) beyond the sort, or O(n) if we copy before sorting to avoid mutating the input. This sort-then-adjacent-check is the lightest member of the merge-intervals family and a frequent warm-up before the full merge.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, a shared settlement resource, such as a single clearing channel, can only be used by one booking at a time, and various desks request booking windows for it. The scheduling system must determine whether any two requested windows clash before confirming the day's bookings, because a clash would mean two desks trying to use the exclusive channel simultaneously. This is exactly the any-overlap existence problem.

Problem 2 — Checking every pair of bookings is quadratic and too slow when many desks submit windows. Sorting by start and checking only adjacent windows answers the clash question in n log n time, which keeps the booking-confirmation step fast.

The code has the shared `Account` class, an `Interval` class for a booking window, a `BookingConflictChecker` service with a `hasConflict` method implementing sort-then-adjacent-check, and a runnable `OverlappingIntervalsDemo` main class that checks Rajesh's and Priya's booking sets, logging the detected clash at fine level and the yes-or-no result at info level.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's bookings are [9,11], [14,16], [10,12]. First we sort by start, which gives [9,11], [10,12], [14,16]. We walk from the second interval.

Step 1: Compare the second interval [10,12] to the previous [9,11]. The current start 10 is strictly less than the previous end 11, so they overlap, which is a conflict. We log the clash and return true immediately.

The checker returns true because the bookings [9,11] and [10,12] clash on the shared resource.

For Priya the sorted bookings are [9,11], [11,13], [13,15]. Comparing [11,13] to [9,11], the current start 11 is not strictly less than the previous end 11, so touching is allowed and there is no conflict. Comparing [13,15] to [11,13], the current start 13 is not strictly less than the previous end 13, so no conflict. The checker returns false.

sections.s6_takeaway:
This problem asks whether any two intervals in a set overlap, a simple yes or no, and I solve it in n log n time by sorting the intervals by start value and then checking only adjacent pairs. The naive all-pairs comparison is quadratic, but once the intervals are in start order, any overlap surfaces between an interval and its immediate predecessor, because if an earlier-starting interval overlaps a later one, the later one begins before the earlier one ends, which I catch by comparing each interval's start to the previous interval's end.

I walk the sorted list from the second interval, and if any current start is strictly less than the previous end I return true immediately. I use strictly less than so that touching intervals, where one ends exactly as the next begins, count as non-overlapping, which fits booking windows where back-to-back use is allowed; if the domain treats touching as a clash I switch to less than or equal to. Comparing the current start to the previous end also correctly catches a fully contained interval, because a contained interval starts before its enclosing interval ends.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the settlement scheduler. A shared settlement resource like a single clearing channel could only be used by one booking at a time, and before confirming the day's bookings the system had to determine whether any two requested windows clashed, since a clash meant two desks trying to use the exclusive channel at once. Sorting the windows by start and checking only adjacent pairs answered the clash question in n log n time, which kept booking confirmation fast even when many desks submitted windows.

The senior-level point I make is that sorting collapses an all-pairs question into a single adjacency scan, which is the same enabling insight as the full merge-intervals problem, making this the lightweight warm-up of that family. I also stress the deliberate choice between strict and non-strict comparison for touching intervals, since that is a real domain decision rather than a detail, and I note that the containment case is handled for free by comparing against the previous end. Framing this as the existence-only cousin of merge intervals and calling out the touching-policy decision is what tells an interviewer I understand the whole family rather than one isolated problem.
